units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS

Certainly. Whenever you like. I’m going to look in at the Bachelors’ Ball to-night, unless I find something better to do. But I’ll come round to-morrow morning. If you should want me to-night by any chance, send round a note to Curzon Street.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Thank you.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: As he reaches the door , LADY CHILTERN enters from her boudoir .
You are not going, Robert?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I have some letters to write, dear.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Going to him .
You work too hard, Robert. You seem never to think of yourself, and you are looking so tired.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: It is nothing, dear, nothing.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: He kisses her and goes out .
To LORD GORING.

Do sit down. I am so glad you have called. I want to talk to you about . . . well, not about bonnets, or the Woman’s Liberal Association. You take far too much interest in the first subject, and not nearly enough in the second.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: You want to talk to me about Mrs. Cheveley?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes. You have guessed it. After you left last night I found out that what she had said was really true. Of course I made Robert write her a letter at once, withdrawing his promise.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: So he gave me to understand.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: To have kept it would have been the first stain on a career that has been stainless always. Robert must be above reproach. He is not like other men. He cannot afford to do what other men do.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: She looks at LORD GORING, who remains silent .

Don’t you agree with me? You are Robert’s greatest friend. You are our greatest friend, Lord Goring. No one, except myself, knows Robert better than you do. He has no secrets from me, and I don’t think he has any from you.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: He certainly has no secrets from me. At least I don’t think so.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Then am I not right in my estimate of him? I know I am right. But speak to me frankly.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Looking straight at her .
Quite frankly?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Surely. You have nothing to conceal, have you?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Nothing. But, my dear Lady Chiltern, I think, if you will allow me to say so, that in practical life—
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Smiling .
Of which you know so little, Lord Goring—
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Of which I know nothing by experience, though I know something by observation. I think that in practical life there is something about success, actual success, that is a little unscrupulous, something about ambition that is unscrupulous always. Once a man has set his heart and soul on getting to a certain point, if he has to climb the crag, he climbs the crag; if he has to walk in the mire—
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Well?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: He walks in the mire. Of course I am only talking generally about life.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Gravely .
I hope so. Why do you look at me so strangely, Lord Goring?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Lady Chiltern, I have sometimes thought that . . . perhaps you are a little hard in some of your views on life. I think that . . . often you don’t make sufficient allowances. In every nature there are elements of weakness, or worse than weakness. Supposing, for instance, that—that any public man, my father, or Lord Merton, or Robert, say, had, years ago, written some foolish letter to some one . . .
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What do you mean by a foolish letter?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: A letter gravely compromising one’s position. I am only putting an imaginary case.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Robert is as incapable of doing a foolish thing as he is of doing a wrong thing.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: After a long pause .
Nobody is incapable of doing a foolish thing. Nobody is incapable of doing a wrong thing.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Are you a Pessimist? What will the other dandies say? They will all have to go into mourning.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Rising .

No, Lady Chiltern, I am not a Pessimist. Indeed I am not sure that I quite know what Pessimism really means. All I do know is that life cannot be understood without much charity, cannot be lived without much charity. It is love, and not German philosophy, that is the true explanation of this world, whatever may be the explanation of the next. And if you are ever in trouble, Lady Chiltern, trust me absolutely, and I will help you in every way I can. If you ever want me, come to me for my assistance, and you shall have it. Come at once to me.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Looking at him in surprise .
Lord Goring, you are talking quite seriously. I don’t think I ever heard you talk seriously before.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Laughing .
You must excuse me, Lady Chiltern. It won’t occur again, if I can help it.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: But I like you to be serious.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Enter MABEL CHILTERN, in the most ravishing frock .
